items.title: Les Gets World Cup Breakdown | €100K Won & A French Fairytale
items.description:
Hattie Harnden just won the €100,000 Gates Belted Purse, Max Alran took his first Elite World Cup victory in front of an incredible home crowd, and Les Gets delivered another absolutely wild weekend of downhill racing.

After a six-week break, Chris is joined by Olly Morris and Neko Mulally to break down everything that happened at the Les Gets UCI Downhill World Cup.

At the centre of the women's race was Hattie Harnden. In constantly changing conditions, Hattie found the speed and lines she needed to take her first Elite Downhill World Cup victory and, with it, finally secure the €100,000 Gates Belted Purse for AON Racing.

It's also a significant moment technically. Hattie's AON bike uses a belt-driven gearbox drivetrain and a radically different approach to weight distribution and setup. Winning at Les Gets proves that concept can deliver at the very highest level of World Cup downhill racing.

We dig into Hattie's run, the crucial line choices that made the difference and what the result means for AON, before looking across a stacked women's race that also saw Vali Höll secure the 2026 World Cup overall with two rounds still remaining.

Then there's Max Alran.

Fastest in timed training, winner of Q1 and last man down the mountain at his home World Cup, Max delivered when it mattered. He crossed the line 1.650 seconds ahead of Andreas Kolb to claim his first Elite World Cup victory as the Les Gets hillside erupted around him.

We break down Max's incredible weekend alongside Andreas Kolb, Jackson Goldstone, Richie Rude, Antoine Pierron, Amaury Pierron, Jordan Williams and the developing men's overall battle.

There's plenty more too, including the extraordinary weather that transformed the track, brutal qualifying conditions, tyre and setup decisions, practice limitations, the rapidly changing lines riders faced during finals and standout performances across the Junior fields.

From Hattie's €100k breakthrough and Max's home victory to Vali wrapping up the overall, this was another reminder of why Les Gets continues to produce some of the most memorable racing on the World Cup calendar.

Next stop: the 2026 UCI Mountain Bike World Championships in Val di Sole.

items.title: Henri Kiefer: Why Speed Isn't Enough to Win
items.description:
Henri Kiefer already knows he has the speed to compete with the fastest downhill racers in the world.

The harder challenge has been learning how to access that speed when the pressure is highest.

In this episode of the Downtime Podcast, Henri joins Chris to talk about confidence, expectation, visualisation and the mental side of racing at the very top of World Cup downhill.

We rewind to the 2025 World Championships in Champéry, where Henri arrived with an unusually strong sense of belief and produced one of the biggest rides of his career. At just 20 years old, he took Elite World Championship silver, with only Jackson Goldstone able to beat his time.

Henri explains how GoPro footage, visualisation and confidence helped him prepare, and why he believes a World Championship demands an almost extreme level of self-belief.

From there, we go back through his journey from grassroots racing in Germany and the iXS Rookies Cup to the SRAM Young Guns programme, Canyon, and his relationship with three-time World Champion Fabien Barel.

We discuss Henri's 2023 Junior World Championship victory, his move into Elite racing and the difficult transition from being one of the fastest juniors in the world to lining up against riders he'd spent years watching.

Henri also opens up about the highs and lows of his 2025 season, including mechanicals, missed qualifications, his first Elite World Cup podium, World Championship silver and a run of podium performances that suddenly made everything feel effortless.

Then came injury.

A scaphoid fracture at Mont-Sainte-Anne disrupted his off-season and contributed to a difficult start to 2026. But as Henri explains, the physical setback wasn't the whole problem.

He'd become too focused on results, comparison and what he believed he should be achieving.

Working with Fabien, his coach and his father, Henri began changing the way he approached race weekends. The shift quickly paid off with another podium at Leogang and a return to greater consistency.

Throughout the episode, we get into visualisation, routines, reflection, confidence, learning from teammates like Troy Brosnan and Luca Shaw, and the delicate balance between ambition and pressure.

Henri has already been Junior World Champion, stood on Elite World Cup podiums and finished within touching distance of an Elite rainbow jersey.

The speed isn't the question anymore.

The challenge is creating the conditions that allow that speed to appear when it matters most.

items.title: "Why I Raced 100 Miles With A Broken Wrist" Kate Courtney on Just Ride
items.description:
Kate Courtney explains how a wrist injury unexpectedly led her to one of the biggest breakthroughs of her career.

After stepping away from World Cup racing, Kate took on the iconic Leadville 100, a 100-mile mountain bike race at high altitude, despite having limited preparation and recovering from injury.

She reflects on how removing expectations, embracing a completely different challenge, and focusing on learning rather than results helped her rediscover her motivation and ultimately chase a record-setting ride.

items.title: Why Downhill Racing Changed After Aaron Gwin | Just Ride
items.description:
Aaron Gwin changed downhill mountain biking.

With five overall World Cup titles and 20 World Cup wins, the American brought a new level of speed to the sport, finding lines others couldn't see and producing some of the most iconic runs in downhill history.

Aaron joins Rob Warner and Eliot Jackson on Just Ride to look back at the races that defined his career, including his legendary chainless run, the secrets behind his dominant years and his rivalry with Greg Minnaar.

He also opens up about the brutal run of injuries that disrupted the second half of his career, why he stepped away from running his own team to focus purely on racing again, and what it's like now sharing a team with rising American star Asa Vermette.

Plus, Aaron reveals what finally convinced him to race Red Bull Hardline, why it transformed his confidence on a bike and why, at 38, he still believes he has the speed to fight for a World Cup podium.

🎧 This is Aaron Gwin on Just Ride.

items.title: Mountain Bikers Don't Train HARD ENOUGH 🥵 Ronan Dunne on Just Ride
items.description:
Does mountain biking have a training problem?

In this clip from the Just Ride podcast, Ronan Dunne compares downhill mountain biking and motocross, arguing that riders often don't spend enough time on the bike and that the sport could benefit from a stronger training culture.

Alongside Rob Warner and Eliot Jackson, Ronan discusses training volume, bike park habits, recovering from injury, and whether too much practice can actually hurt race performance.
